# California Freelance Design Startup Checklist

## Legal Setup for a Home-Based Sole Proprietor
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/house.svg

- **Start date:** 2026-03-01
- **Business type assumed:** solo freelance graphic design from home
- **Expected revenue:** about **$4,000/month** initially
- **Core goal:** stay simple at first, but cover registration, tax, contracts, and liability basics

## Sole Proprietorship vs. LLC for Your Situation
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/building.svg

| Topic | Sole Proprietorship | LLC |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Easiest and cheapest | More filing and annual maintenance |
| Liability | No personal liability shield | Better separation of business and personal assets |
| Taxes | Usually simplest; income reported on personal return | Can be taxed similarly at first; more flexibility later |
| Credibility | Fine for small solo work | Often looks more formal to clients |
| Ongoing admin | Minimal | More compliance and recordkeeping |
| Best fit here | Good if you want to start fast and keep costs low | Better if you want extra liability protection and a more formal structure |

### Practical takeaway
- If you want the **lowest-cost, fastest start**, begin as a **sole proprietor**.
- If you want **stronger liability separation** from day one, form an **LLC** before or soon after launch.
- For a freelance designer with moderate early income, the biggest difference is usually **legal protection**, not day-to-day taxes.

## California Registration, Tax, Contract, and Liability Checklist
Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/check2-square.svg

| Step | What to do | Why it matters | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Choose your business name | Confirms how you’ll market and invoice | Before launch |
| 2 | Check name availability | Avoid conflicts with existing businesses | Before using the name |
| 3 | File a DBA if needed | Required if you use a name other than your legal name | Before branding publicly |
| 4 | Register an LLC if chosen | Creates the legal entity and separation | Before or near launch |
| 5 | Get an EIN if useful | Helps with banking, forms, and client onboarding | Before opening accounts or hiring |
| 6 | Open a business bank account | Keeps business and personal funds separate | At start |
| 7 | Track income and expenses | Needed for taxes and deductions | From day 1 |
| 8 | Set aside estimated taxes | Helps cover federal and California tax bills | Monthly or quarterly |
| 9 | Use written client contracts | Defines scope, payment, rights, and deadlines | Before each project |
| 10 | Review insurance needs | Reduces risk from claims, mistakes, or disputes | Early in business |

### Registration notes
- As a **sole proprietor**, you may still need a **DBA/Fictitious Business Name** if you operate under a name other than your legal name.
- If you form an **LLC in California**, expect extra state filing and annual compliance.
- If you work from home, check whether your **city or county** requires a local business license or home-occupation permit.

### Tax notes
- Your freelance income is generally reported on your personal return, and you may need to make **estimated tax payments**.
- At roughly **$4,000/month**, you should plan for:
  - **federal income tax**
  - **self-employment tax**
  - **California state income tax**
- Keep a simple system for:
  - client invoices
  - software subscriptions
  - hardware and supplies
  - home office costs, if eligible
  - mileage and business travel, if any

### Contract essentials
Use a written agreement for every client, even small jobs. Include:
- scope of work
- deliverables and revision limits
- timeline and milestones
- payment schedule and late fees
- ownership/licensing of final artwork
- client-provided content responsibilities
- cancellation, kill fee, and change-order terms
- approval process and file handoff details

### Liability protection basics
- Use a separate business bank account.
- Keep project files, invoices, and contracts organized.
- Consider **general liability** and **professional liability / errors & omissions** insurance.
- If you use contractors later, confirm classification and paperwork before paying them.
